title: Episode 332: Queen Elizabeth II (Part 1): Accession at Tree Tops, the Coronation of 1953, and the Decolonization of Empire
description:
The radiant dawn of the second Elizabethan era: the youth, marriage, dramatic accession, and crowning of Queen Elizabeth II. Born third in line to the throne, Princess Elizabeth never expected to rule until the 1936 abdication altered destiny. During World War II, the teenage princess insisted on serving in uniform as a mechanic and truck driver in the Auxiliary Territorial Service. In 1947, she made her famous twenty-first birthday broadcast dedicating her 'whole life, whether it be long or short' to the imperial service, and married the handsome naval lieutenant Prince Philip Mountbatten. When King George VI died in February 1952, twenty-five-year-old Elizabeth was watching wildlife from the branches of a giant fig tree at Tree Tops in Kenya—becoming the first monarch since the Hanoverians to accede while overseas. Her breathtaking 1953 coronation launched the television age, while her tireless Commonwealth diplomacy navigated the winds of decolonization.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series chronicles the opening decades of the longest and most celebrated reign in British history: Queen Elizabeth II. Here is George with the extraordinary story of the young princess who acceded in a Kenyan treetop and transformed the ancient monarchy for the modern television age.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: PRINCESS LILIBET AND THE WARTIME ATS DRIVER: 1926 TO 1945
Born on April 21, 1926, at 17 Bruton Street in London's Mayfair, Princess Elizabeth Alexandra Mary—known within her family as 'Lilibet'—was the eldest daughter of the Duke and Duchess of York. When her grandfather King George V fell seriously ill in 1928, little Lilibet's precocious, cheerful presence at his bedside was credited with reviving the old King's spirits, while Winston Churchill famously remarked after meeting the two-year-old princess that she possessed 'an air of authority and reflectiveness astonishing in an infant'. Educated at home in constitutional history by Henry Marten, the Vice-Provost of Eton College, Elizabeth grew up with a deep, instinctive reverence for constitutional law and duty. During the London Blitz, she and her younger sister Princess Margaret lived at Windsor Castle, sleeping in subterranean dungeons during air raids. In October 1940, at age fourteen, Elizabeth made her first radio broadcast on the BBC's Children's Hour, reassuring thousands of evacuated children: 'In the end, all will be well; for God will care for us and give us victory and peace.' Determined to participate directly in the national war effort, Elizabeth badgered her father until he granted her permission to join the Auxiliary Territorial Service in early 1945. Registered as Second Subaltern Elizabeth Windsor, number 230873, the future queen wore grease-stained overalls, learned to strip and rebuild heavy truck engines, drive military ambulances, and change giant wheels, proving her willingness to share the common labor of her generation. On VE Day, May 8, 1945, nineteen-year-old Elizabeth and her sister Margaret received permission from their parents to slip out of Buckingham Palace incognito to celebrate with the jubilant crowds. Pulling her ATS uniform cap low over her eyes, the future Queen danced the conga through the Ritz Hotel and linked arms with ordinary Londoners in Trafalgar Square, shouting 'We want the King!' in what she later called 'one of the most memorable nights of my life.'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: PHILIP MOUNTBATTEN AND THE ROYAL WEDDING: 1947
Princess Elizabeth's heart had been won years earlier in July 1939, when, as a thirteen-year-old girl visiting the Royal Naval College at Dartmouth, she was escorted by an eighteen-year-old naval cadet of dazzling blond good looks: Prince Philip of Greece and Denmark. Philip was a descendant of Queen Victoria through his mother, Princess Alice of Battenberg, but his family had been exiled from Greece in turmoil, leaving him impoverished, homeless, and raised by British relatives. During World War II, Philip served with distinction in the Royal Navy, mentioned in dispatches for his heroism during the Battle of Cape Matapan. Elizabeth and Philip exchanged letters throughout the war, and upon his return to London, the young couple fell deeply in love. Courtiers initially viewed Philip with snobbish skepticism, grumbling that he was rough-mannered, penniless, and had German brothers-in-law, but Elizabeth's determination was unshakeable. In April 1947, during a royal tour of South Africa on her twenty-first birthday, Elizabeth broadcast a solemn, immortal pledge to the worldwide Commonwealth: 'I declare before you all that my whole life, whether it be long or short, shall be devoted to your service and the service of our great imperial family to which we all belong.' On November 20, 1947, Elizabeth married Philip—created Duke of Edinburgh—at Westminster Abbey. In postwar Britain, still gripped by severe bread and clothes rationing, the royal wedding was a magical splash of color, with Winston Churchill describing it as 'a flash of colour on the hard road we have to travel'.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: TREE TOPS, KENYA, AND THE MIDNIGHT ACCESSION: FEBRUARY 1952
In early 1952, with King George VI recovering from lung surgery, Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip departed on a grand tour of East Africa, Australia, and New Zealand on his behalf. On the afternoon of February 5, 1952, the royal party arrived at Tree Tops Hotel in Kenya, a rustic wooden lodge built high in the branches of an ancient giant fig tree overlooking a natural waterhole in the Aberdare National Park. Elizabeth spent an enchanted night watching herds of wild elephants, rhinos, and baboons gather beneath the tree, filming the magnificent scene with her personal cine-camera and marveling at the African sunrise. Naturalist Jim Corbett, who served as the royal party's armed bodyguard, famously wrote in the hotel guestbook: 'For the first time in the history of the world, a young girl climbed into a tree one day a Princess, and after having what she described as her most thrilling experience, she climbed down from the tree next day a Queen.' Miles away at Sandringham, King George VI died in his sleep in the early morning hours. News of the King's death was relayed through London and Nairobi to Prince Philip, who gently broke the shattering news to his wife beside a trout stream at the nearby Sagana Lodge. Twenty-five-year-old Elizabeth displayed extraordinary composure: when her private secretary Martin Charteris asked what regnal name she wished to assume, she replied simply: 'My own name, of course—Elizabeth.' She immediately began writing letters of apology to the leaders of Australia and New Zealand for cancelling the remainder of her tour. Landing at London Airport dressed in mourning black, the young Queen was met at the aircraft steps by Prime Minister Winston Churchill, Clement Attlee, and Anthony Eden, bearing the weight of the British Crown upon her youthful shoulders.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE CORONATION OF 1953 AND THE TELEVISION REVOLUTION
Queen Elizabeth II's coronation at Westminster Abbey on June 2, 1953, was a landmark spectacle that fundamentally transformed mass communications and heralded the television age. The Coronation Commission, chaired by eighty-year-old Winston Churchill and the Queen's grandmother Queen Mary, initially opposed allowing television cameras inside the sacred Abbey, arguing that sacred religious rites should not be treated as popular theatrical entertainment. But Prince Philip, who chaired the coronation planning committee, championed modern technology, and Queen Elizabeth firmly overruled Churchill, insisting that all her subjects should be able to witness their sovereign take the solemn oaths. Over twenty million people in the United Kingdom watched the coronation live on television, crowding around tiny, nine-inch black-and-white screens in living rooms, village halls, and church basements, while tens of millions more listened on the radio across six continents. Despite unseasonal summer rain, three million people lined the London streets as the glittering Gold State Coach carried the twenty-seven-year-old Queen to Westminster Abbey. Inside the Abbey, the holy moment of anointing—when the Archbishop of Canterbury touched consecrated oil onto the Queen's hands, breast, and head—was shielded from the cameras beneath a golden canopy of cloth of gold, preserving the ancient, mystical spiritual covenant between the sovereign and God. That very morning, news arrived that a British expedition led by John Hunt, with Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay, had reached the summit of Mount Everest, sparking euphoric national celebration that a glorious new Elizabethan Age had dawned. In the weeks leading up to the ceremony, the young Queen had practiced wearing the nearly five-pound St. Edward's Crown during her daily desk work, wearing it while taking tea and reviewing state papers so that her neck muscles would not falter beneath the sacred weight during the three-hour coronation ritual, demonstrating the meticulous professionalism that would define her seven-decade reign.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE GLOBAL COMMONWEALTH TOUR AND THE SUEZ CRISIS: 1953 TO 1956
Immediately following her coronation, Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip embarked on a grueling, unprecedented six-month world tour of the Commonwealth, covering over forty-three thousand miles by steamship, train, and aircraft across Bermuda, Jamaica, Fiji, Tonga, New Zealand, Australia, Ceylon, Uganda, and Malta. In Australia, an astounding three-quarters of the entire continent's population turned out to see their young Queen in person, an outpouring of imperial warmth never equaled in history. Yet this glittering imperial harmony was soon shattered by the geopolitical convulsions of the Cold War. In October 1956, Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal, prompting British Prime Minister Sir Anthony Eden to orchestrate a secret, disastrous Anglo-French-Israeli military invasion to seize back the canal. The Suez Crisis was an unmitigated disaster: furious diplomatic and financial pressure from United States President Dwight D. Eisenhower forced Britain into a humiliating military retreat, shattering Britain's illusion of being an independent global superpower and forcing Eden's resignation. Through this humiliating national crisis, Queen Elizabeth maintained scrupulous constitutional neutrality, advising her ministers in private while recognizing that Britain's future lay not in military empire, but in the voluntary, egalitarian partnership of the expanding Commonwealth of Nations.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE WINDS OF CHANGE: DECOLONIZATION AND THE NEW COMMONWEALTH: 1960 TO 1970
The 1960s witnessed the rapid, breathtaking dissolution of the British Empire as dozens of former colonies across Africa, the Caribbean, and Asia gained full independence. When Prime Minister Harold Macmillan delivered his famous 'Wind of Change' speech to the South African parliament in February 1960, warning that African national consciousness was an unstoppable force, Queen Elizabeth embraced decolonization not with bitter imperial regret, but with visionary enthusiasm for the modern Commonwealth. In November 1961, despite grave security warnings from the British cabinet that Marxist President Kwame Nkrumah might be targeted for assassination, the Queen courageously proceeded with a state visit to Ghana. At a state ball in Accra, Elizabeth famously danced the foxtrot with President Nkrumah, a radiant, electrifying gesture of multiracial partnership that destroyed apartheid propaganda, delighted African leaders, and cemented Ghana's decision to remain within the Commonwealth family. Throughout the 1960s, as Ghana, Nigeria, Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Jamaica, and Trinidad gained their independence, Elizabeth embraced each newly independent leader as an equal head of state, transforming the Commonwealth from an imperial relic into a unique, dynamic international forum representing a third of humanity.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE SILVER JUBILEE AND THE MODERN ROYAL FAMILY: 1977
In 1977, Great Britain celebrated Queen Elizabeth II's Silver Jubilee, marking twenty-five years on the throne. The milestone occurred against a bleak backdrop of economic stagflation, three-day working weeks, soaring inflation, industrial strikes, and violent sectarian conflict in Northern Ireland, leading skeptical commentators to predict that the Jubilee would be a sullen, embarrassing failure. Instead, the Silver Jubilee unleashed an astonishing wave of genuine national celebration: over one million people packed the Mall to cheer the Queen on Jubilee Day, while more than twelve thousand street parties transformed working-class neighborhoods across London, Manchester, and Glasgow into sea of red, white, and blue bunting. The Queen and Prince Philip traveled twelve thousand miles across Britain, meeting over a million citizens in person. Even the rebellious counterculture of the punk explosion—epitomized by the Sex Pistols' satirical single 'God Save the Queen'—could not diminish the deep, affectionate respect ordinary citizens felt for the steadfast woman who had served them without complaint for a quarter of a century. At a Guildhall luncheon in London, Elizabeth reaffirmed her lifelong dedication: 'When I was twenty-one, I pledged my life to the service of our people and I asked for God's help to make good that vow. Although that vow was made in my salad days, when I was green in judgment, I do not regret nor take back one single word.'

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Silver Jubilee reaffirmed Queen Elizabeth II as the bedrock of British identity, but stormy seas lay ahead. Join us next time for the grand finale of our Kings and Queens of England series: the fairytale wedding of Prince Charles and Lady Diana Spencer, the trials of the Annus Horribilis, seventy magnificent years of service culminating in the Platinum Jubilee, and the accession of King Charles III. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
